Syllabus: Evolution & basic characteristics · Pre-British period · Economy till 2008 & after 2008 · Structural changes · Issues facing the economy (poverty, jobless growth, inequality, migration, pressure on resources, remedies, pandemics). PYQs mostly test terms and characteristics.

1. Basic characteristics

  • India is a mixed economy: public and private sectors coexist.
  • It is a developing, lower-middle-income economy (World Bank groups: low, lower-middle, upper-middle, high).
  • Large population and young demographic profile (demographic dividend).
  • Agriculture's share of output has fallen, but it still employs the largest share of workers.
  • Services now produce more than half of GVA.
  • Large informal (unorganised) workforce; regional disparities; low per-capita income.

2. Evolution

PhaseFeatures
Pre-BritishA prosperous, self-sufficient village economy of agriculture and handicrafts (textiles, metalwork). It held a large share of world output and strong export trade ("golden sparrow")
British ruleDe-industrialisation (handicrafts ruined by machine-made imports); drain of wealth (Dadabhai Naoroji, Poverty and Un-British Rule in India); commercialisation of agriculture; zamindari and land-revenue systems; railways (1853) built for raw-material export. At independence: stagnant agriculture, low literacy, low life expectancy, mass poverty
1951–1991Planned, state-led mixed economy; import substitution; licence-permit raj; ~3.5% growth = the "Hindu rate of growth" (Prof. Raj Krishna, 1978)
1991–2008LPG reforms after the BoP crisis; faster growth, peaking near 9% in 2005–08; IT and services boom
After 2008Global financial crisis → fiscal and monetary stimulus; 2013 taper tantrum; twin balance-sheet problem (stressed corporates + NPAs); IBC 2016; demonetisation 2016; GST 2017; COVID contraction 2020-21, then recovery; India among the fastest-growing major economies

3. Structural change

As an economy develops, the shares of output and jobs shift from primary → secondary → tertiary. India jumped largely from agriculture to services. Agriculture's share of GDP fell from over half in 1950-51 to under a fifth. Services became the largest sector, and manufacturing stayed relatively low (one reason for jobless growth).

4. Growth terms

TermMeaning
V-shaped recoverySharp fall, then an equally quick rebound
U / W / L / KU: slow bottoming. W: double dip. L: prolonged stagnation. K: some sectors recover while others stagnate
Jobless growthOutput grows but employment stagnates or falls
Capital formationInvestment in productive assets; needed for growth
Make in India (Sept 2014)4 pillars: new processes, new infrastructure, new sectors, new mindset

5. Issues facing the economy (book list)

  • Poverty:
    • Poverty lines from the Tendulkar and Rangarajan committees.
    • NITI Aayog's Multidimensional Poverty Index (health, education, standard of living — 12 indicators).
    • Remedies: MGNREGA (100 days of wage work), NRLM-DAY, PMAY, PM-KISAN, food security (NFSA / PMGKAY).
  • Jobless growth: capital-intensive growth, slow manufacturing. Remedies: labour-intensive manufacturing, MSMEs, Skill India, PLI.
  • Rising inequality (income, wealth, regional; Gini). Remedies: progressive taxes, DBT, inclusive finance (PMJDY).
  • Migration and pressure on resources: rural–urban migration, urban congestion, water and land stress.
  • Pandemics: COVID-19 supply shock and demand collapse. Response: Atmanirbhar Bharat package, ECLGS, free food grains, moratorium and restructuring.
The COVID recovery was uneven. Financial, real-estate and professional services and public administration crossed pre-pandemic levels first. Trade, hotels, transport and communication recovered only gradually.

1. Meaning and history

Economic planning: a central authority sets targets and allocates resources over a period to reach defined goals.

  • Pre-independence plans:

    • INC's National Planning Committee under Nehru (1938).
    • Bombay Plan (industrialists, 1944).
    • Gandhian Plan (S.N. Agarwal, 1944).
    • People's Plan (M.N. Roy, 1945).
    • Sarvodaya Plan (J.P. Narayan, 1950).
  • Planning Commission: 15 March 1950, by a Cabinet resolution (non-statutory, extra-constitutional), chaired by the PM. National Development Council: 1952. India's model drew on the Soviet one.

2. Objectives and types

  • Objectives: growth, employment, poverty alleviation, reduced inequality, self-reliance, modernisation, price stability, balanced regional development. Not profit maximisation of private firms.
  • Types:
    • Imperative (directive; command economies) vs indicative (state indicates goals and the private sector is guided by incentives — India from the 8th plan).
    • Centralised vs decentralised.
    • Perspective (long-term) vs fixed vs rolling (annually revised).
    • Physical vs financial planning.
    • Democratic vs totalitarian.
  • Achievements: food self-sufficiency, an industrial base, infrastructure, institutions (IITs, IIMs, DFIs), higher literacy and life expectancy. Failures: unemployment, poverty, inequality, low efficiency of PSUs.
  • Financial resources: domestic budgetary resources (largest — taxes, PSU surpluses), domestic borrowing, deficit financing (borrowing from RBI, drawing down cash balances, borrowing from the public and foreign governments), external assistance. Not forex reserves.

3. NITI Aayog (1 January 2015)

  • National Institution for Transforming India; replaced the Planning Commission. Also created by Cabinet resolution.
  • Chairperson: the PM, with a Vice-Chairperson and a CEO.
  • Governing Council: all Chief Ministers and the Lt Governors of UTs.
  • A think tank for cooperative and competitive federalism and bottom-up (village-level) planning. Monitors the SDGs; Atal Innovation Mission; indices (SDG India Index, MPI, Export Preparedness).
  • Replaced five-year plans with a 15-year vision, 7-year strategy and 3-year action agenda.
  • It does not allocate funds to states; the Finance Ministry and Finance Commission handle devolution.
"To allocate resources to the states" is the classic NOT-a-function-of-NITI option. The Planning Commission was not a statutory body. The 12th plan was the last.

1. In simple words

Some sectors create lots of jobs but find it hard to get bank credit: small farmers, tiny enterprises, poor households, students. RBI therefore makes banks lend a minimum share of their credit to them. That share is Priority Sector Lending.

Branch example: a KCC crop loan to a 2-acre farmer counts toward the agriculture target and the small & marginal farmer sub-target. A ₹40 lakh loan to a micro manufacturing unit counts as MSE/micro lending.

  • It cuts costs and raises productivity, so it has a multiplier effect on growth.

Syllabus: Globalisation and its advocacy · Impact on India · Fair globalisation & the need for a policy framework · Globalisation in reverse gear — re-emergence of protectionism.

1. Meaning and advocacy

Globalisation = integration of national economies through flows of goods and services, capital, technology, people and information.

  • Drivers: lower trade barriers (GATT/WTO), technology (internet, containers), MNCs, capital-account liberalisation.
  • Advocates argue: efficiency through comparative advantage, larger markets, technology transfer, cheaper goods for consumers, FDI and jobs.

2. Impact on India (post-1991)

PositiveNegative / concerns
Higher growth; IT/ITES and services exports; FDI and FPI inflows; strong forex reserves; consumer choice; technology upgrades; integration into global value chainsRising inequality; agrarian distress; competition hurting small firms; volatility from capital flows (contagion — 2008, 2013); jobless growth; environmental stress; dependence on imports (electronics, energy)

3. Fair globalisation

  • The ILO World Commission on the Social Dimension of Globalization (2004 report, "A Fair Globalization") said globalisation should create opportunities for all.
  • Its elements: economic development + liberalisation + social development (decent work) + environmental conservation + inclusion and good governance. Not privatisation as such.
  • Needed: national policy frameworks (social protection, skills), fair global trade rules, accountable institutions.

4. Reverse gear — protectionism

  • Protectionism = shielding domestic producers through tariffs, import quotas, non-tariff barriers (standards, licensing), subsidies, anti-dumping duties, currency manipulation. GST is a domestic tax, not protectionism.
  • Signs of de-globalisation ("slowbalisation"):
    • 2008 crisis and the post-crisis slowdown in trade.
    • Brexit (2016).
    • US–China trade war (2018 on) and the 2025 US "reciprocal" tariffs.
    • WTO dispute settlement stalled (Appellate Body non-functional since Dec 2019).
    • COVID supply-chain shocks.
    • Reshoring, friend-shoring, "China+1".
  • India's response: Atmanirbhar Bharat, PLI schemes, selective tariff increases, plus bilateral FTAs (UAE CEPA 2022, Australia ECTA 2022, EFTA TEPA — in force Oct 2025, UK CETA — signed July 2025).
A7:
Syllabus: Overview · Transformation of the real sector · Financial sector · Integration with the global economy · Economic reforms in India.

1. Why 1991

  • BoP crisis: forex reserves covered only about 2 weeks of imports, high fiscal deficit and inflation. The Gulf War raised oil prices and cut remittances, and NRI deposits fled. India pledged gold and borrowed from the IMF.
  • Jagdish Bhagwati's three failures:
    1. Extensive bureaucratic controls.
    2. Inward-looking trade and FDI policy.
    3. Inefficient public sector.
  • Reform model: LPG — Liberalisation, Privatisation, Globalisation. Two parts: stabilisation (short-term demand management — fiscal deficit, inflation) and structural reforms (long-term supply side).
  • Book's LPG era: 1992–2008.

2. Real sector

  • New Industrial Policy (24 July 1991):
    • Industrial licensing abolished except for a few industries.
    • Sectors reserved for the public sector cut from 17 to 8, now 2: atomic energy and railway operations.
    • MRTP restrictions removed; later replaced by the Competition Act 2002 (CCI).
    • Automatic route for FDI.
    • Disinvestment of PSUs.
  • Tax reforms (Chelliah Committee): lower and simpler rates, VAT → GST (2017).
  • Agricultural reforms were slower: MSP and procurement, e-NAM, PM-KISAN.

3. Financial sector

  • Narasimham Committee I (1991):
    • Cut SLR and CRR.
    • Deregulate interest rates.
    • Prudential norms (income recognition, asset classification, provisioning; capital adequacy).
    • Entry of private banks (1993 guidelines).
    • Debt Recovery Tribunals.
  • Narasimham II (1998): stronger banking system, mergers of strong banks, the narrow-bank concept for weak banks.
  • Capital market: SEBI made statutory (1992), Capital Issues Control abolished, NSE (1994), dematerialisation, FPIs allowed.
  • Later: SARFAESI 2002, IBC 2016, inflation targeting 2016.

4. Integration with the global economy

  • Rupee devalued in July 1991 (two steps) → LERMS (1992, dual rate) → unified market-determined rate (1993).
  • Current-account convertibility (Aug 1994; IMF Article VIII).
  • Peak customs duties sharply reduced; quantitative restrictions phased out.
  • FEMA 1999 replaced FERA 1973 (civil, not criminal).
  • FDI and FPI liberalised; ECBs allowed.
  • High-Level Committee on BoP (1991–93): C. Rangarajan. Tarapore Committees on capital-account convertibility (1997, 2006).
Second-generation reforms: GST, IBC, the monetary policy framework, DBT/JAM, the labour codes, PLI, privatisation of Air India (2022).
The aim of the 1991 reforms was higher growth with lower CAD and inflation — not "to nationalise banks" (that was 1969/1980). FEMA replaced FERA, not the reverse.

Syllabus: FTP — structural changes in the 1990s · FTP 2015-20 · challenges for the next FTP · FDI, FII and recent trends · Economic development vs growth. 30 PYQs.

1. Foreign Trade Policy

  • Framed by the Ministry of Commerce (DGFT) under the Foreign Trade (Development & Regulation) Act, 1992.
  • 1990s structural change: before 1991 India was protected by high tariffs, licences and quotas. From 1991 came lower tariffs, removal of licensing and quantitative restrictions, a market-based rupee and EXIM policies — a sharp break from protectionism.
  • FTP 2015-20 (extended to March 2023):
    • MEIS — duty-credit scrips of 2–5% of FOB value for goods.
    • SEIS — for services.
    • Both were replaced by RoDTEP (2021), which refunds embedded taxes such as electricity duty and mandi tax, and RoSCTL for garments.
  • FTP 2023 (1 Apr 2023, no end date):
    • Four pillars: Incentive to Remission; Export promotion through Collaboration (states, districts, Indian missions); Ease of Doing Business; Emerging Areas (e-commerce, Districts as Export Hubs, SCOMET).
    • Target: $2 trillion of exports by 2030.
    • Also: an amnesty scheme for EPCG/AA defaults, international trade in INR, and new Towns of Export Excellence.
  • Niryat Bandhu (DGFT): mentoring and outreach for new and potential exporters (no subsidies).
  • Challenges for the next FTP: WTO-compatibility of incentives, protectionism abroad, logistics cost, services exports, FTAs, CBAM and other green barriers.

3. FII / FPI

  • Portfolio investment in shares and bonds: short-term "hot money", hedge funds, volatile, can exit quickly. Registered with SEBI (FPI Regulations 2019).
  • An FPI may hold below 10% of a company's equity. At 10% or more, the holding is treated as FDI.
  • FDI is long-term, builds productive capacity and brings technology and management.
  • VRR (Voluntary Retention Route, RBI 2019): FPIs get relaxed debt-investment norms if they retain the investment for a minimum period.

4. Economic growth vs development

GrowthDevelopment
Quantitative rise in real national output/incomeQualitative improvement in living standards, poverty, health, education, equality

Developing economy indicators: low per capita income and productivity, high population growth, a large share of labour in agriculture, unemployment, poverty and low human development. A highly diversified, technologically advanced industry marks a developed economy.

  • Development is multi-dimensional.

Syllabus: IMF and World Bank · WTO — India and WTO · Regional economic cooperation · Recent international economic issues.

1. Bretton Woods institutions (conference July 1944; HQ Washington DC)

BodyKey facts
IMF (1945)
  • Roles: surveillance (Article IV consultations), BoP lending with conditionality, technical assistance, SDR allocation. Not a world central bank. Publishes the World Economic Outlook and Global Financial Stability Report.
  • Members contribute quotas, which decide voting and access. The USA has a veto on key decisions (> 15% vote). India is a founder member.
  • SDR (1969): a supplementary reserve asset and the IMF's unit of account — neither a currency nor a claim on the IMF. Basket: USD, EUR, CNY, JPY, GBP (CNY added 2016).
World Bank Group
  • IBRD (1944): loans to middle-income countries.
  • IDA (1960): soft loans and grants to the poorest.
  • IFC (1956): private sector.
  • MIGA (1988): political-risk guarantees, not loans.
  • ICSID (1966): investment disputes — India is not a member.
  • Voting is by shares plus basic votes.

World Bank-supported in India: Swachh Bharat, Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan, PMKSY, National Ganga River Basin, NRLM.

2. WTO (1 January 1995, Geneva)

  • Replaced GATT (1947); India is a founder member of both.
  • Highest body: the Ministerial Conference (at least every 2 years); then the General Council.
  • Functions: administers agreements (GATT, GATS, TRIPS, TRIMs, SPS, Agreement on Agriculture), negotiation forum, dispute settlement, trade-policy review. It does not finance BoP or guarantee loans.
  • Principles: non-discrimination — Most-Favoured-Nation (treat all members equally) and national treatment (imports treated like local goods once inside) — plus transparency and special and differential treatment for developing countries.

A10:
Syllabus: Core elements of sustainable development · Global issues & initiatives · India's progress on SDGs incl. climate change · CSR activities. 30 PYQs — CSR alone was asked in 6 sessions.

1. Sustainable development and SDGs

  • Sustainable development (Brundtland Report, 1987): development that meets present needs without compromising the ability of future generations to meet theirs. Three pillars: economic growth, social inclusion, environmental protection.
  • SDGs ("Transforming our World: the 2030 Agenda"):
    • Adopted by the UN General Assembly in Sept 2015; in force 1 Jan 2016 – 2030.
    • 17 goals, 169 targets. They replaced the 8 MDGs (2000–2015).
    • Built on the 5 Ps: People, Planet, Prosperity, Peace, Partnership.
  • Selected goals: 1 No Poverty · 2 Zero Hunger · 3 Good Health · 4 Quality Education · 5 Gender Equality · 6 Clean Water & Sanitation · 7 Affordable & Clean Energy · 8 Decent Work & Economic Growth · 9 Industry, Innovation & Infrastructure · 11 Sustainable Cities · 13 Climate Action · 14 Life below Water · 15 Life on Land · 17 Partnerships.
  • India: NITI Aayog coordinates and publishes the SDG India Index; MoSPI owns the indicator framework. CSR activities map onto SDGs 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 and others.

2. Climate change — global and India

  • UNFCCC (1992) → Kyoto Protocol (1997) → Paris Agreement (COP-21, 2015): keep warming well below 2°C and pursue 1.5°C, through nationally determined contributions (NDCs).
  • India's Panchamrit (COP-26, Glasgow 2021):
    1. 500 GW of non-fossil capacity by 2030.
    2. 50% of energy requirements from renewables by 2030.
    3. Cut projected emissions by 1 billion tonnes by 2030.
    4. Cut the carbon intensity of the economy by 45% by 2030 (updated NDC: 45% below 2005 levels).
    5. Net zero by 2070.
  • Also from India: International Solar Alliance (2015, HQ Gurugram); OSOWOG (One Sun One World One Grid — a global solar grid, launched at COP-26 with the Green Grids Initiative); Mission LiFE; Plastic Hackathon target of no single-use plastic by 2022; Green Credit Programme and Carbon Credit Trading Scheme (2023).
  • RBI and banks:
    • Sustainable Finance Group in the Department of Regulation (2021), to suggest strategies and regulation for sustainable practices and climate risk.
    • Green Deposit framework (2023): deposits allocated to renewable energy, energy efficiency, clean transport, climate adaptation, pollution control. Fossil fuels, nuclear and large hydro are excluded.
    • Green bonds (most with 5–10 year tenors; also issued by the World Bank for Indian projects); Sovereign Green Bonds (2023).
  • ESG: environmental, social and governance criteria used by responsible investors to screen investments. Good governance serves all stakeholders over the long term, not just short-term shareholders.

3. CSR — Sec 135, Companies Act 2013 (Schedule VII)

PointRule

SpendAt least 2% of average net profit of the 3 immediately preceding financial years. If the average is negative → nil. Excess spend can be set off over the next 3 years

Worked example: profits (₹ lakh) of 250, 275 and 300 → average 275 → CSR = ₹5.5 lakh. Profits of 300, −200, 200 → average 100 → ₹2 lakh. If the average is negative → nil.

  • Net zero is 2070, not 2050.
  • SDGs = 17 goals and 169 targets, adopted by the UNGA (not UNDP).
  • CSR uses the average of 3 years, not 2 or 5.
  • Breach of CSR rules is a civil wrong.
  • Green deposits exclude fossil-fuel projects.

Syllabus: Economics — an introduction · Microeconomics and macroeconomics · Types of economies: market, command, mixed.

  • Economics studies how society uses scarce resources with alternative uses to satisfy unlimited wants. The central problems are what to produce, how to produce, and for whom.

  • Microeconomics: individual units — consumer, firm, price of a good. It assumes perfect competition and rational behaviour, which is its main limitation.
  • Macroeconomics: aggregates — GDP, unemployment, inflation, money supply. Its "father" is J.M. Keynes ("General Theory", 1936, written after the Great Depression).
  • Positive economics describes "what is"; normative economics says "what ought to be".

B2:
Syllabus: Demand schedule · Forces behind the demand curve · Shifts in demand · Supply schedule & forces · Shifts in supply · Equilibrium · Effect of shifts · Interpreting price & quantity changes.

Demand

  • Demand schedule: a table of the quantity bought at each price. Law of demand: price ↑ → quantity demanded ↓ (other things constant), so the demand curve slopes downward.
  • Why it slopes down: the substitution effect (a dearer good is replaced by cheaper substitutes) and the income effect (a higher price lowers real income). Diminishing marginal utility also contributes.
  • Exceptions:
    • Giffen goods — inferior staples whose demand rises with price (Robert Giffen).
    • Veblen goods — prestige goods, "conspicuous consumption" (Thorstein Veblen).
    • Expectations of further price rises.
  • Forces (determinants): own price, consumers' income, prices of related goods (substitutes and complements), tastes, population, expectations.
  • Movement along the curve = change in the good's own price. Shift of the whole curve = change in any other factor.

Supply

  • Supply schedule and curve: price vs quantity producers are willing to sell. It slopes upward.
  • Shifts come from input costs, technology, prices of other goods, taxes/subsidies, number of sellers, weather.

Equilibrium and shifts

ChangeEquilibrium priceEquilibrium quantity
Demand ↑ (shift right)↑↑
Demand ↓↓↓
Supply ↑ (shift right)↓↑
Supply ↓ (shift left)↑↓

Interpreting data: if price and quantity rise together, demand has shifted. If price falls while quantity rises, supply has shifted.

Equilibrium calculation: Qd = 100 − 4P and Qs = 28 + 2P. Set them equal: 100 − 4P = 28 + 2P → P = 12. Then Q = 100 − 48 = 52.
A fall in the good's own price causes a movement, not a shift. Demand depends on income too. "Substitution effect only" is wrong — both effects work.
B3:
Syllabus: What is money · Money supply · Inflation · Causes of inflation · Measures of inflation.

1. Money

  • Functions: primary — medium of exchange (removes the need for a double coincidence of wants) and measure of value. Secondary — store of value and standard of deferred payment. Money does not itself create production capacity.
  • Kinds: commodity money; fiat money (value by government order — our notes); fiduciary money (based on trust — cheques, drafts); legal tender (must be accepted — notes and coins).
  • Issue: RBI issues all banknotes except the ₹1 note. The Government of India issues the ₹1 note and mints all coins. Notes can legally be issued up to ₹10,000. ₹2000 notes were withdrawn from circulation in May 2023 but remain legal tender.

2. Money supply measures (RBI)

MeasureCompositionName
M0Currency in circulation + bankers' deposits with RBI + other deposits with RBIReserve / base / high-powered money
M1Currency with public + demand deposits with banks + other deposits with RBINarrow money (most liquid)
M2M1 + savings deposits with post office savings banks
M3M1 + time deposits with banksBroad money (most used)
M4M3 + all deposits with post office savings organisation (excluding NSCs)Broadest, least liquid
  • Money multiplier = M3 ÷ M0 (Friedman & Schwartz). A higher CRR means a lower multiplier.
  • Velocity of money = Nominal GDP ÷ M3 — how many times a rupee is spent on output in a year.
  • Sources of M3 = net bank credit to government + bank credit to the commercial sector + net foreign exchange assets of the banking sector + government's currency liabilities to the public − net non-monetary liabilities of the banking sector.

3. Inflation — meaning and types

Inflation is a sustained rise in the general price level, meaning the purchasing power of money falls.

By speedRate (indicative)
CreepingBelow 3% a year
Walking / trotting3–10%
Running / gallopingDouble digits
HyperinflationExtremely high (e.g., 50%+ a month)
By causeWhat drives itExample
Demand-pullAggregate demand rises faster than supply ("too much money chasing too few goods")Big government spending plus tax cuts; credit boom
Cost-pushCosts of key inputs rise where there are no suitable substitutesCrude-oil spike; wage push; monsoon failure in food
Built-in / structuralWage-price spiral, supply bottlenecksAgriculture or infrastructure constraints
  • Headline = all items. Core = headline minus food and fuel (volatile items).
  • Deflation: the price level falls (negative inflation). Disinflation: inflation is positive but falling (6% → 4%). Stagflation: high inflation + stagnant growth + unemployment. Reflation: deliberate policy to lift prices and output after a slump.
  • Who gains from unexpected inflation: borrowers and the Government (debt). Who loses: lenders, depositors, fixed-income earners and pensioners.
  • Real interest rate ≈ nominal rate − inflation (Fisher). An FD at 7% with 5.1% inflation earns about 1.9% real.

4. Measures of inflation

IndexCompiled byKey facts
CPI (Rural, Urban, Combined)NSO, MoSPIMonthly. Retail prices of goods and services. CPI-C is RBI's target measure. new base year 2024 (new series from Feb 2026). Food has the largest weight
WPIOffice of the Economic Adviser, DPIITMonthly. Wholesale goods only (no services). Weights: manufactured products ~64%, primary articles ~23%, fuel & power ~13%
CPI-IW / CPI-AL / CPI-RLLabour BureauFor industrial workers (DA revision) and agricultural/rural labourers
GDP deflatorNSO(Nominal GDP ÷ Real GDP) × 100. The broadest measure, covering all domestically produced goods & services. Quarterly
Inflation rate from an index = (Current − Previous) ÷ Previous × 100. CPI from 125 to 130 → 5 ÷ 125 = 4%.

5. Controlling inflation

  • Monetary: raise repo/CRR, sell G-secs (OMO), tighten liquidity.
  • Fiscal: cut government spending, raise taxes, reduce the deficit.
  • Supply-side: imports, buffer stocks, removing bottlenecks.
Traps:
  • Demand-pull comes from increasing demand.
  • Cost-push applies where no substitutes exist.
  • WPI has no services.
  • Coins are issued by the Government, not RBI.
  • M1 is narrow and M3 is broad; M2 and M4 add post-office money.
  • Velocity uses nominal GDP.

Inflation falls from 6% to 4%. Deflation or disinflation?Disinflation (prices still rising, just slower).
Which index does RBI target?CPI-Combined (rural + urban).
B4:
Syllabus: Classical theory · Keynes' liquidity preference · Money demand curve · Equilibrium in the money market · Effect of increase in money supply · Shifts in liquidity preference · Hicks-Hansen IS-LM.

TheoryInterest is the price of…Determined byKey names
Classical ("demand and supply theory of capital")Saving / capitalDemand for investment = supply of savings. Interest is the reward for waiting/abstinenceMarshall, Fisher, Pigou
Loanable funds (neo-classical)Loanable fundsDemand and supply of loanable funds (savings + bank credit + dishoarding)Robertson, Ohlin
Liquidity preferenceParting with liquidityDemand for money and supply of moneyJ.M. Keynes (critic of the classical theory)

Keynes: why people hold money

  • Transactions motive: day-to-day spending; depends on income.
  • Precautionary motive: emergencies; also depends on income.
  • Speculative motive: to profit from future bond-price changes; depends inversely on the rate of interest.
  • The money demand (liquidity preference) curve slopes downward against the interest rate. The money supply is fixed by RBI (vertical). Their intersection gives the equilibrium interest rate.
  • Money supply ↑ → interest rate ↓ (until the liquidity trap, where people hold any extra money and the rate cannot fall further).
  • Income ↑ → money demand shifts right → interest rate ↑.

IS-LM (Hicks-Hansen synthesis of Keynesian theory)

  • IS curve: goods-market equilibrium (Investment = Saving). Downward-sloping in (income, interest) space.
  • LM curve: money-market equilibrium (Liquidity preference = Money supply). Derived from Keynes' liquidity preference theory. Upward-sloping.
  • The intersection fixes equilibrium income and interest rate together.
  • Fiscal policy (government spending, taxes) shifts IS; monetary policy (money supply) shifts LM.
There is no "preference motive". The LM curve comes from liquidity preference, NOT the classical theory. Government spending moves IS, not LM.
B5:
Syllabus: Characteristics and phases of a business cycle. Asked in every session (1 mark each time).

  • Business (trade) cycles are recurring, wave-like fluctuations in output, employment, income and prices around the long-run trend.
  • Characteristics: recurring/periodic, wave-like, synchronic (sectors move together), pervasive (spread across the economy and abroad), cumulative, and with varying duration. "Non-pervasive" is NOT a feature.
PhaseSigns
Expansion / BoomAccelerated, prolonged demand growth; demand exceeds sustainable output; the economy overheats; demand-supply lag; rising prices, wages, credit and investment
PeakFull capacity, growth at its maximum; turning point
Recession (comes right after the boom)Demand turns down; sales fall and unplanned inventories build up; investment and credit demand fall; inflation low or falling
Depression / troughExtremely low aggregate demand; prices at their lowest; unemployment rises sharply; inflation very low
RecoveryOutput, employment and income start rising; confidence and investment return
  • Indicators:
    • Leading — PMI, new orders, stock prices.
    • Coincident — IIP, GDP.
    • Lagging — unemployment rate, interest rates.
  • Policy responses: in a recession, rate cuts and fiscal stimulus; in a boom, tightening.
  • Recovery shapes: V (sharp fall, sharp rebound), U, L (long stagnation), K (divergent sectors), W (double dip).
B6:
Syllabus: Tools of monetary policy · How monetary policy in India responded to the Global Financial Crisis · Fiscal policy & FRBM (see B8). This is the highest-frequency chapter in the PYQs (45 questions, asked in all 7 sessions).

1. In simple words

Monetary policy is how RBI controls the cost and quantity of money in the economy, so that prices stay stable while growth continues. RBI does this mainly by changing the rate at which banks borrow from it (the repo rate) and by adding or removing liquidity (cash) from banks.

Branch example: RBI cuts repo by 25 bps. Your bank's EBLR-linked home loans (repo + spread) reset lower at the next reset, which must be within 3 months. Deposit rates follow with a lag. More borrowing → more spending → growth. The reverse happens when RBI hikes.

2. The framework (RBI Act, amended 2016)

  • Objective (Preamble / Sec 45ZA): price stability while keeping growth in mind — Flexible Inflation Targeting (FIT), recommended by the Urjit Patel Committee (2014) and adopted in 2016.
  • Target: CPI-Combined inflation of 4% ± 2% (band 2–6%). It is set by the Central Government in consultation with RBI, every 5 years. new Retained for 1 Apr 2026 – 31 Mar 2031.
  • Failure = inflation outside the band for 3 consecutive quarters. RBI then reports to the Government with reasons, remedial action and a timeline (Sec 45ZN).
  • MPC (Sec 45ZB), formed in 2016, has 6 members:
    • 3 from RBI: the Governor (chair), the Deputy Governor in charge of monetary policy, and one RBI officer nominated by the Central Board.
    • 3 external members appointed by the Government, for 4 years with no re-appointment.
    It meets at least 4 times a year (in practice 6). Quorum is 4. Decisions are by majority; in a tie the Governor has a casting vote. Minutes are published on the 14th day. Members keep a silent period from 7 days before to 7 days after each meeting.

3. Tools of monetary policy

Quantitative (general)Qualitative (selective)
CRR, SLR, Bank Rate, repo / reverse repo / SDF (LAF), MSF, OMOs, MSS, LTRO/TLTRO, VRR/VRRR, forex swapsMargin requirements on loans against goods/shares, selective credit control, credit rationing, moral suasion, direct action
ToolMeaningKey facts
RepoRBI lends to banks against G-secs (sell now, buy back later)Policy rate. Injects liquidity. 5.25% (June 2026)
SDF (Apr 2022)Banks park surplus with RBI without collateralFloor of the corridor, 5.00%. The SDF balance counts for SLR. Replaced the fixed reverse repo as the floor
Reverse repoRBI borrows from banks giving G-secs as collateralAbsorbs liquidity. Kept at 3.35%, no longer the floor
MSF (May 2011)Overnight borrowing by SCBs when the market is tightCeiling, 5.50%. Banks may dip into SLR up to 2% of NDTL. A "safety valve"
Bank RateRediscount / long-term lending rate (the "discount rate")Aligned to MSF (5.50%). Penal rates are linked to it
CRR% of NDTL kept as cash with RBIRBI Act Sec 42. 3% (cut from 4% in 4 tranches, Sep–Nov 2025). No interest, no floor or ceiling. Fortnightly average, with at least 90% on every day

MSS (2004)Special T-bills/dated securities issued to sterilise surplus liquidity, e.g., from forex inflowsProceeds are kept in a separate account, not spent by the Government
LTRO / TLTRO (2020)Long-term repos at the repo rateTenors 1 & 3 years. TLTRO funds went to corporate bonds/CP/NCDs; TLTRO 2.0 required 50% in small/mid NBFCs & MFIs

Corridor picture: SDF 5.00 ← Repo 5.25 → MSF / Bank Rate 5.50 (each ±25 bps). Stance: neutral (June 2026). FY27 projections: GDP 6.6%, CPI 5.1%.

4. Lending-rate benchmarks (transmission)

  • BPLR (2003) → Base Rate (2010) → MCLR (1 Apr 2016) → EBLR (1 Oct 2019).
  • MCLR = marginal cost of funds + negative carry on CRR + operating costs + tenor premium. It is published for overnight, 1M, 3M, 6M and 1Y (no 2-month MCLR). Lending rate = MCLR + spread.
  • EBLR is mandatory for new floating-rate retail and MSE loans. Benchmark options: RBI repo, FBIL 3-month T-bill, FBIL 6-month T-bill, or another FBIL benchmark. The rate must reset at least once in 3 months.
  • MCLR and BPLR are bank-level rates, not RBI policy rates.

5. How monetary policy responded to the Global Financial Crisis (2008-09)

  • Repo cut from 9% to 4.75% (Oct 2008 – Apr 2009); reverse repo from 6% to 3.25%.
  • CRR cut from 9% to 5%; SLR from 25% to 24%.
  • Special liquidity windows: special repo for banks to fund MFs and NBFCs, refinance to SIDBI, NHB and EXIM, a forex swap window for banks' overseas branches, and relaxed ECB/FCNR rules.
  • Lesson: conventional rate cuts plus targeted liquidity. The same approach was reused in COVID-19 (LTRO, TLTRO, moratorium).
Traps:
  • CRR is RBI Act 42 and SLR is BR Act 24 — examiners swap them.
  • The MSF rate is ABOVE repo.
  • RBI pays NO interest on CRR.
  • The target is set by the Government, not RBI.
  • SDF needs no collateral, but the reverse repo does.
  • Hawkish = tightening.
  • Repo injects liquidity; reverse repo and SDF absorb it.

B7:
Syllabus: National income & GDP concepts — computation, utility. 21 PYQs, asked in all 7 sessions; the most frequent home of calculation questions.

1. In simple words

GDP is the market value of all final goods and services produced within the country in a year. Everything else is an adjustment to it:

  • Gross → Net: subtract depreciation.
  • Domestic → National: add net factor income from abroad (NFIA).
  • Market price → Factor cost: subtract indirect taxes and add subsidies.

2. The formula ladder

AggregateFormula
GDP at market prices (GDPmp)C + I + G + (X − M)
GNPmpGDPmp + NFIA
NDPmpGDPmp − Depreciation (consumption of fixed capital)
NNPmpGNPmp − Depreciation = GDPmp + NFIA − Depreciation
… at factor cost… at MP − Indirect taxes + Subsidies
National IncomeNNP at factor cost
Per capita incomeNational income ÷ population
GVA at basic pricesValue of output − Intermediate consumption
GVA at factor costGVA(basic) − Production taxes + Production subsidies
GDPmpGVA(basic) + Product taxes − Product subsidies
GDP deflatorNominal GDP ÷ Real GDP × 100
  • Nominal GDP = current prices. Real GDP = constant (base-year) prices.
  • Personal income → minus direct taxes → personal disposable income.

3. Three methods of computation

MethodAdds up
Production / value-addedGVA of all sectors (output − intermediate consumption). Avoids double counting
IncomeCompensation of employees + operating surplus (rent, interest, profit) + mixed income of the self-employed (+ production taxes, depreciation to reach GDP)
ExpenditurePrivate final consumption + government final consumption + gross capital formation + net exports
  • In India the NSO (MoSPI) compiles GDP. Estimates come out in stages: advance estimates (Jan), provisional estimates (end-May), and quarterly estimates about 2 months after each quarter.
  • new Base year 2022-23 (series released 27 Feb 2026), replacing 2011-12. The new series uses GST, PFMS and e-Vahan data, double deflation and supply-use tables.
  • IIBF book / May 2023 key: GDP in India is "mainly calculated using the expenditure method". Know this keyed answer, though NSO's primary estimate is production-side.

4. Utility and limitations

  • Uses: measuring growth and the size of the economy, comparing countries and periods, per capita welfare, sector shares, guiding fiscal and monetary policy and planning, the base for ratios (deficit/GDP, debt/GDP, credit/GDP).
  • Limitations: ignores non-market work (household services), the informal sector is hard to capture, says nothing about distribution, ignores environmental damage and leisure, and has price-base problems.
Practise these:
  • GDPmp 1000, Dep 0.05, IT 5, Sub 3 → NDPfc = 1000 − 0.05 − 5 + 3 = 997.95.
  • GDPmp 22, NFIA 3, Dep 2.4 → NNPmp = 22.6.
  • Output 875, IC 460, prod. taxes 40, subsidies 15 → GVA(FC) = 390.
  • C 100, I 100, G 200, X 100, M 100 → GDP = 400.
Traps:
  • NFIA is used only for national aggregates, never for domestic ones.
  • Government consumption is an expenditure-method item, not an income item.
  • Transfer payments (pensions, subsidies, scholarships) are not part of GDP.
  • The base year is now 2022-23.

Why use value added instead of total sales?To avoid double counting intermediate goods.
B8:
Syllabus: Fiscal policy & FRBM Act · Union Budget — receipts, expenditure, plan expenditure, deficit concepts. 17 PYQs; calculations asked in Oct 2024 and Nov 2025.

1. Fiscal policy

  • Fiscal policy is the Government's use of taxation and public expenditure (and borrowing) to influence demand, growth, employment, prices and distribution. Keynes made it central to macro-stabilisation.
  • Counter-cyclical: in a slowdown spend more or tax less (expansionary); when overheating spend less or tax more (contractionary).
  • Monetary policy belongs to RBI; fiscal policy belongs to the Government.

2. The Union Budget

  • Constitutionally the Annual Financial Statement (Article 112). Presented on 1 February since 2017; the Railway Budget was merged into it the same year.
  • Government funds:
    • Consolidated Fund of India (Art 266) — all receipts and expenditure.
    • Contingency Fund (Art 267) — emergencies.
    • Public Account — e.g., provident funds and small savings, where the Government is only a banker.
  • The plan / non-plan classification of expenditure was abolished from 2017-18. Expenditure is now classified only as revenue vs capital.
ReceiptsExamples
Revenue — taxDirect: income tax, corporation tax. Indirect: GST (since July 2017; GST 2.0 slabs of 5% and 18% plus 40% demerit rate, from 22 Sept 2025), customs, excise
Revenue — non-taxInterest receipts, dividends & profits (RBI, PSUs), fees, fines, external grants
Capital — debtMarket borrowings (G-secs, T-bills), small savings / securities against them, external loans
Capital — non-debtRecoveries of loans & advances, disinvestment / miscellaneous capital receipts
ExpenditureExamples
RevenueCreates no asset or liability reduction: salaries, pensions, interest, subsidies, grants to states, running of departments
CapitalCreates assets or reduces liabilities: roads, defence capital outlay, loans to PSUs/states, repayment of debt

3. Deficit concepts

DeficitFormula
Revenue deficitRevenue expenditure − Revenue receipts
Effective revenue deficitRevenue deficit − Grants for creation of capital assets
Fiscal deficitTotal expenditure − (Revenue receipts + Non-debt capital receipts) = the total borrowing requirement
Primary deficitFiscal deficit − Interest payments (borrowing needed for current spending, excluding past debt)
Worked example (Nov 2025 PYQ):
  • Revenue receipts = 3.5 + 4.6 + 0.7 + 0.4 = 9.2.
  • Non-debt capital receipts = recoveries 0.3 + disinvestment 0.5 = 0.8.
  • Total expenditure = 4.2 + 2.4 + 1.1 + 1.5 + 2.7 + 0.4 = 12.3.
  • Fiscal deficit = 12.3 − 10.0 = 2.3. Primary deficit = 2.3 − interest 4.2 = −1.9 (a primary surplus).

4. FRBM Act 2003 and the N.K. Singh review

  • Objectives: long-term macro stability with revenue surpluses, prudent debt management, fiscal transparency, a medium-term fiscal framework, and removing fiscal impediments to monetary policy.

Syllabus: What is a financial system · Phase I pre-1951 · Phase II 1951 to mid-eighties · Phase III post-nineties · Narasimham Committee (1991) · Reform of the banking sector (1992–2008) · Present status. 17 PYQs.

1. What is a financial system?

The network that moves savings from those who have surplus money (households) to those who need it (businesses and government). It has four parts:

  • Institutions — banks, NBFCs, insurers, MFs, DFIs.
  • Markets — money, capital, forex, derivatives.
  • Instruments — deposits, shares, bonds, T-bills.
  • Services — payments, advisory, custody.

It also has regulators (RBI, SEBI, IRDAI, PFRDA, IBBI).

  • Formal system: organised, institutional and regulated — regulators, intermediaries, non-intermediaries (DFIs that lend directly to corporates) and other institutions.
  • Informal system: moneylenders, indigenous bankers, chit groups, friends and relatives. Low transaction cost, unstructured procedures, but high interest and no regulation.

2. Phases of development (as per syllabus)

PhaseMain features
I: Pre-1951Largely private, unregulated, urban-centred banking; many bank failures.
  • Presidency banks (Bengal 1806/1809, Bombay 1840, Madras 1843) merged into the Imperial Bank (1921).
  • Hilton Young Commission (1926) recommended a central bank → RBI (1 Apr 1935).
  • Banking Regulation Act 1949; RBI nationalised 1949.
II: 1951 – mid-1980sPlanning era; the state directs credit.
  • Institutions: SBI 1955 (from the Imperial Bank), LIC 1956, DICGC 1962, UTI 1964, IDBI 1964.
  • Nationalisation: 14 banks in 1969, 6 in 1980.
  • Priority sector lending, Lead Bank Scheme (1969), RRBs (1975), NABARD (1982), EXIM (1982).
  • Administered interest rates and high CRR/SLR ("financial repression").
III: Post-1990sLiberalisation.
  • Narasimham Committees; interest rates deregulated; CRR/SLR cut.
  • New private banks (1993); SEBI made statutory (1992); NSE (1992); IRDA (1999).
  • Technology, Basel norms, financial inclusion, payment banks and SFBs (2015-16), IBC (2016).

Some PYQs use a 4-phase version: I pre-independence · II post-independence · III post-liberalisation (1991–2007) · IV post-global financial crisis (2008 onwards). LIC (1956) falls in Phase II in both versions.

3. Narasimham Committee I (1991) — Committee on the Financial System

  • Reduce SLR (from 38.5% to 25% over 5 years) and CRR progressively.
  • Capital adequacy 8% (Basel I) in phases.
  • Prudential norms: income recognition, asset classification, provisioning (IRAC).
  • Deregulate interest rates; phase out directed credit (priority sector to be cut to 10% — not accepted).
  • Abolish branch licensing; free entry of private and foreign banks.
  • 4-tier banking structure:
    1. 3–4 large international banks.
    2. 8–10 national banks.
    3. Local banks.
    4. Rural banks.
  • Asset Reconstruction Fund for bad debts; special tribunals for recovery (→ DRTs, 1993).

4. Banking reforms 1992–2008

  • Prudential norms (IRAC 1992-93; 90-day NPA norm from 2004). CRAR 8% then 9%.
  • Interest deregulation (lending rates freed; BPLR 2003). New private banks: 1993 guidelines (UTI/Axis, ICICI, HDFC…).
  • DRTs (RDDBFI Act 1993); SARFAESI (2002); CIBIL (2000); Lok Adalats; Corporate Debt Restructuring (2001).
  • Technology: core banking, RTGS (2004), NEFT (2005). Basel II from 2008.
  • Narasimham II (1998) — Committee on Banking Sector Reforms: universal banking, mergers of strong banks, higher CRAR (10%), closing weak banks.

5. Present status (2026)

  • 12 PSBs after the 2019–20 mergers (BoB ← Dena + Vijaya; PNB ← OBC + United; Canara ← Syndicate; Union ← Andhra + Corporation; Indian ← Allahabad).
  • Also: private banks, foreign banks, SFBs, payment banks, RRBs (consolidated to 28 from 1 May 2025, "One State One RRB"), co-operative banks.
  • Strong balance sheets, low NPAs, digital public infrastructure (UPI, Account Aggregators).

Traps:
  • Narasimham I said 8% CRAR (not 10%) and a 4-tier structure.
  • Universal banking was Narasimham II.
  • Moneylenders are informal.
  • Andhra, Vijaya and Corporation banks were nationalised in 1980, not 1969.

1. Functions of banks

  • Primary: accepting deposits and lending (BR Act Sec 5(b) defines banking as accepting deposits repayable on demand or otherwise, withdrawable by cheque, for lending or investment).
  • Secondary: agency services (collections, payments, standing instructions) and utility services (lockers, guarantees, LCs, remittances).
  • Para-banking (Sec 6): insurance, MF distribution, DP, cards, merchant banking.

2. Structure

Non-scheduled banksNot in the schedule. Cannot borrow from RBI for normal business. Keep a cash reserve under Sec 18 BR Act, with themselves or in a current account with RBI — not compulsorily with RBI. Weaker regulatory standing than scheduled banks
SCBsPSBs (12), private, foreign (branch or wholly-owned subsidiary), RRBs, SFBs, payment banks

3. Co-operative banks

  • Short-term rural (3-tier): State Co-operative Bank → District Central Co-operative Bank → PACS at village level.
  • Long-term rural: SCARDB → PCARDB (land development banks). These are outside the BR Act.
  • Urban Co-operative Banks: mostly retail lending to individuals and MSMEs in non-rural areas. Limited non-fund and corporate exposure. Most cannot deal in forex directly. Four-tier regulatory framework (2022), PSL 60% (2025).
  • Dual control: registrar of co-operative societies (management) and RBI (banking). The BR (Amendment) Act 2020 strengthened RBI's powers. StCBs and DCCBs are supervised by NABARD.
  • Co-operative banks are the most numerous banks in India.

4. Key RBI guidelines and recent changes

  • Fit-and-proper criteria for directors; ownership caps in private banks (promoter up to 26% after 15 years).
  • new Banking Laws (Amendment) Act 2025: up to 4 nominees per deposit account/locker; "substantial interest" threshold raised from ₹5 lakh to ₹2 crore; longer tenure for co-operative bank directors.
  • Fintech (finance firm using technology, e.g., P2P lending) vs techfin (tech firm offering finance, e.g., WhatsApp Pay). Neo-banks are digital front-ends partnering with licensed banks.
  • NBFCs: see chapter C6.
Traps:
  • Payment banks: ₹2 lakh limit (not ₹1 or ₹3 lakh), no loans.
  • RRB capital split is 50 : 35 : 15 (sponsor 35).
  • SCARDBs are outside the BR Act.
  • WhatsApp Pay = techfin.
  • Scheduled-bank criteria are in the RBI Act (Sec 42(6)).

Syllabus: Evolution of DFIs · Gaps after independence · Objectives · Classification · Role · Changing role and universal banking · IFCI, ICICI, IDBI, SIDBI, EXIM, NABARD, NHB, NaBFID. 26 PYQs, asked in all 7 sessions.

1. Why DFIs?

After 1947 the economy needed long-term finance for industry and infrastructure. Commercial banks mobilise short-term deposits, so long-tenor lending would create an asset-liability mismatch. DFIs were set up to provide:

  • Long-term loans, equity, underwriting and guarantees.
  • Promotional and developmental work: project identification, technical consultancy, entrepreneurship development.
  • Finance for backward regions and priority sectors (balanced regional development) and capital formation.

DFIs do not accept demand deposits. They fund themselves through Government capital, market borrowings (bonds) and lines from multilaterals (World Bank, ADB, IFC).

Today RBI regulates five AIFIs: EXIM Bank, NABARD, NHB, SIDBI and NaBFID.

Created by RBI: IDBI, NABARD (from ARDC), NHB, DICGC. Not by RBI: IFCI, EXIM, ICICI, SIDBI (an IDBI subsidiary).

4. Changing role and universal banks

After 1991, cheap Government and RBI funds (LTO funds, SLR bonds) dried up. DFIs faced market-cost funding, competition from banks and the bond market, and high NPAs. The Khan Working Group (1998) and Narasimham II recommended converting them into universal banks (commercial + development finance) — hence ICICI (2002) and IDBI (2004). Refinance DFIs (NABARD, SIDBI, NHB) stayed, and in 2021 a new DFI, NaBFID, was created for infrastructure.

Traps:
  • The first DFI is IFCI, not IDBI.
  • ICICI was set up at the World Bank's initiative, not RBI's or the IMF's.
  • EXIM lends to sovereign governments through Lines of Credit.
  • UTI is an investment institution, not a specialised FI.
  • SIDBI is a DFI; SEBI is a regulator; SBI is a bank.

Syllabus: Evolution of microfinance · Grameen Bank model · Delivery of microfinance · SHG-Bank Linkage · JLGs · Regulatory framework · Bank finance to MFIs as PSL · RBI Microfinance Directions 2022 · Fair Practices Code for NBFC-MFIs.

1. Concept and evolution

Microfinance is small, collateral-free credit plus savings, insurance and remittances for low-income households and their micro-enterprises. Loans to large corporates are not microfinance.

  • India: the SHG-Bank Linkage Programme (NABARD pilot, 1992); growth of NGO and NBFC MFIs in the 2000s.
  • The Andhra Pradesh crisis (2010) → Malegam Committee (2011) → the NBFC-MFI category.
  • Small Finance Banks (2015) — several were MFIs.
  • Harmonised RBI Directions (2022) for all lenders.

2. Delivery models

ModelFeatures
Grameen model (Muhammad Yunus, Bangladesh)Groups of 5, mostly women. Weekly meetings and repayments. Peer pressure and joint responsibility instead of collateral
SHG10–20 members (minimum 5 in hilly, desert, sparse areas). Homogeneous, mostly poor (BPL). Save first, then on-lend internally, then get a bank loan as a group
JLG (NABARD 2006)4–10 members, often tenant farmers or oral lessees. Individual loans with a mutual guarantee
Individual lendingDirectly to individuals

SHG-BLP models:

  • I — the bank forms and finances SHGs.
  • II — SHGs are formed by NGOs/agencies and financed directly by banks (the most common).
  • III — the bank lends through an NGO/MFI acting as financial intermediary.

SHG loans are PSL and weaker-section lending, collateral-free, and 100% refinanced by NABARD. DAY-NRLM gives interest subvention to women's SHGs.

3. Types of MFIs

Not-for-profit (NGO societies/trusts, Sec 8 companies) · Mutual benefit (co-operatives, MACS) · For-profit (NBFC-MFIs).

4. RBI (Regulatory Framework for Microfinance Loans) Directions, 2022 — applies to all regulated entities

  • Microfinance loan = a collateral-free loan to a household with annual income up to ₹3 lakh (rural and urban alike).
  • Total loan repayments (EMIs) of the household ≤ 50% of monthly household income.
  • No prepayment penalty. No collateral, not even a lien on deposit accounts. Board-approved pricing policy. Simplified fact sheet.
  • NBFC-MFI: new qualifying (microfinance) assets ≥ 60% of total assets (cut from 75% in June 2025). NOF glide path to ₹10 crore by March 2027.
  • Bank loans to MFIs for on-lending qualify as PSL, subject to conditions.

5. Fair Practices Code (NBFC-MFIs)

  • Transparent pricing with an all-inclusive rate in a KFS.
  • Loan cards in the local language.
  • No coercive recovery; recovery only at designated places and times.
  • Grievance redressal officer; training of field staff; credit bureau checks before lending.
Traps:
  • The income limit is ₹3 lakh for all areas.
  • The repayment cap is 50% (not 40% or 75%).
  • SHG refinance is 100%, not 90%.
  • SHG members should be poor, not APL.
  • "Green MFIs" is not a category.

Syllabus: What is an NBFC · Evolution · Role in inclusive growth · Regulators · Classification & types · Owned Fund & NOF · Bank finance to NBFCs · Fair Practice Code · Ombudsman · Scale-Based Regulation. 17 PYQs.

1. Definition

  • A company registered under the Companies Act whose principal business is lending, investment in securities, hire purchase, leasing, insurance, chit business or receiving deposits (RBI Act Sec 45-I).
  • Principal business ("50-50") test: financial assets > 50% of total assets AND income from financial assets > 50% of gross income.
  • Unlike banks, NBFCs cannot accept demand deposits, are not part of the payment & settlement system (cannot issue cheques on themselves), and their deposits are not DICGC-insured.
  • Role: last-mile credit for MSMEs, vehicles, gold, microfinance, housing and consumer durables; financial inclusion; diversify credit sources ("shadow banking" — credit intermediation outside banks).

2. 1997 amendment to Chapter IIIB of the RBI Act

  • A Certificate of Registration from RBI and minimum NOF became mandatory (45-IA).
  • NBFC-Ds must keep liquid assets in unencumbered approved securities (45-IB).
  • Every NBFC must transfer ≥ 20% of profit to a reserve fund (45-IC).
  • RBI got powers to issue directions and file winding-up petitions.

  • NOF for NBFC-ICC, MFI and Factor raised to ₹10 crore by 31 March 2027 (₹5 crore by March 2025). P2P and AA: ₹2 crore.
  • Owned Fund = paid-up equity + preference shares compulsorily convertible to equity + free reserves + share premium + capital reserve − accumulated losses − intangible assets − deferred revenue expenditure.
  • NOF = Owned Fund − investments in and loans to group/subsidiary companies in excess of 10% of the Owned Fund.

6. Deposit-taking NBFCs

Public deposits for 12 to 60 months; none repayable on demand. Interest paid or compounded at rests no shorter than monthly. No gifts or incentives. Deposits are not insured. 15% liquid assets. Very few NBFC-Ds remain.

  • Fair Practices Code: KFS and all-in cost, no harassment in recovery, written sanction in vernacular.

  • NBFC deposits run 12–60 months and are NOT insured.
  • Chit funds are regulated by State Governments.

Syllabus: History & development · Privatisation & FDI · Insurance business globally and in India · Penetration & density · Insurers in India · Legislation · Intermediaries · Reinsurance · Insurance repositories / e-Insurance Account. 18 PYQs (with D12).

1. History

  • First life insurer in India: Oriental Life (Kolkata, 1818). First Indian-owned: Bombay Mutual (1870). The Insurance Act was passed in 1938.
  • Life insurance nationalised → LIC, 1 Sept 1956, with ₹5 crore capital from the Government.
  • General insurance nationalised by the GIBNA Act (1972) → GIC plus 4 subsidiaries (National, New India, Oriental, United India).
  • Malhotra Committee (1993-94) → IRDA Act 1999 (IRDA set up in 2000) → private and foreign entry.
  • FDI limit: 26% → 49% (2015) → 74% (2021) → 100% automatic for insurers and intermediaries (insurance laws amended in 2025; notified May 2026). LIC's cap is 20%.
  • In insurers with foreign investment, at least one of the Chairperson, MD or CEO must be a resident Indian.

2. Legislation

Insurance Act 1938 · LIC Act 1956 · GIBNA 1972 · IRDA Act 1999 · Insurance Laws (Amendment) Acts 2015 and 2025.

IRDAI (Sec 4 IRDA Act): Chairperson + 5 whole-time + 4 part-time members. HQ Hyderabad. Vision: "Insurance for All by 2047".

3. Market measures

  • Insurance penetration = premium ÷ GDP × 100 (about 3.7% for India).
  • Insurance density = premium ÷ population (US$ per head).
  • Example: premium $127 bn, population 141.1 crore → density ≈ $90.
  • India's segments: life (LIC plus private insurers), general, standalone health, specialised (ECGC, AIC) and reinsurance (GIC Re = national reinsurer, plus foreign reinsurer branches).

5. Reinsurance

  • "Insurance of insurers."
  • It adds underwriting capacity, stabilises results, spreads catastrophe risk and protects the balance sheet. It does not remove all of the insurer's risk.
  • Facultative = risk by risk. Treaty = automatic for a class of business. Proportional or non-proportional (excess of loss).
  • An obligatory cession goes to GIC Re.

6. Insurance repositories and the e-Insurance Account (eIA)

  • Launched on 16 Sept 2013. Repositories: NSDL Database Mgmt, Central Insurance Repository (CDSL), SHCIL Projects, KFin (Karvy) and CAMS.
  • The eIA is free, has a unique number and login, and holds all types of policies (life, health, motor, general).
  • It can be opened even without an existing policy.

1. Bad bank: NARCL + IDRCL

A "bad bank" takes large stressed loans off banks' books so that banks can focus on fresh lending.

  • NARCL (National Asset Reconstruction Co., Budget 2021): an ARC that buys large NPAs (₹500 crore+). It pays 15% in cash and 85% in Security Receipts, guaranteed by the Government of India. PSBs hold 51%.
  • IDRCL (India Debt Resolution Co.): the service/operating company that manages and resolves the assets, using market professionals. PSBs and PSFIs hold up to 49%; private lenders the rest.
  • Benefits: frees bank balance sheets and capital, aggregates exposures for faster resolution, and creates a market for stressed assets.
  • Other ARCs are regulated by RBI under SARFAESI (minimum NOF ₹300 crore). ARCIL was the first ARC (2002).

2. Infrastructure financing

  • Features: huge investment, long gestation, economies of scale, externalities. Banks face an asset-liability mismatch (short-term deposits vs long-term loans).
  • Channels: Government budgets, DFIs (NaBFID, IIFCL 2006), banks, NBFC-IFCs, insurance and pension funds, bonds, InvITs, Infrastructure Debt Funds.
  • National Infrastructure Pipeline (₹111 lakh crore); National Monetisation Pipeline.

3. NaBFID (NaBFID Act 2021)

  • A statutory DFI for infrastructure with both financial and developmental objectives:
    • Lending, refinancing and guarantees for infrastructure located wholly or partly in India.
    • Developing the bond, loan and derivatives markets.
  • Authorised capital ₹1 lakh crore (shares of ₹10). The Government initially held 100%, and must always hold at least 26%.
  • Others who may hold shares: multilateral institutions, sovereign wealth funds, pension/insurance funds, banks.
  • Raises money through bonds and loans; does not accept public deposits. Finances private projects as well as public ones.
  • Regulated by RBI as an AIFI. The board includes some independent directors.

4. EASE (Enhanced Access & Service Excellence)

  • A PSB reform agenda launched in 2018 (EASE 1.0) with IBA and BCG. Aim: institutionalise CLEAN and SMART banking.
  • The EASE Index scores each PSB on 120+ objective metrics.
  • Themes:
    • 1.0 — governance, prudential lending, customer responsiveness, credit off-take, financial inclusion, digital.
    • 2.0 and 3.0 — smart lending, tech-enabled banking.
    • 4.0 and later — customer-centric digital banking.
NaBFID has both financial and developmental goals (not "only developmental"). NARCL buys; IDRCL resolves. 15 : 85, not 20 : 80.

1. In simple words

The money market is where funds are borrowed and lent for up to one year. Banks use it to manage day-to-day cash: a branch network collects deposits unevenly, CRR must be met every day, and the treasury borrows or lends overnight to balance the books. It is regulated by RBI, under Chapter IIID of the RBI Act (Sec 45W).

Treasury example: on reporting Friday your bank is ₹500 crore short of CRR. The dealer borrows in the call market overnight, or borrows through TREPS against G-secs, or, as a last resort, uses MSF at 5.50%.

2. Call, notice and term money (all uncollateralised)

SegmentTenor
Call moneyOvernight (1 day)
Notice money2 to 14 days
Term money15 days to 1 year
  • Participants (borrow and lend): scheduled commercial banks (other than RRBs), co-operative banks (other than land development banks) and Primary Dealers. NBFCs, MFs, insurers and corporates cannot participate. They use TREPS / market repo instead.
  • Rates are market-determined. Deals are on NDS-Call or reported within 15 minutes.
EntityBorrowing limit
SCBsIIBF book / PYQ key: borrowing up to 100% of capital funds (fortnightly daily average) and 125% on any day. Current RBI Directions (2021): SCBs use Board-approved limits within the inter-bank liability norms; the 100%/125% limits are now written for SFBs and Payments Banks. No lending limit is prescribed.
Primary Dealers225% of NOF (end of previous year), daily average
Co-operative banks2% of aggregate deposits (end of previous year)

3. Treasury Bills

  • Short-term GoI debt issued by RBI through auctions, as zero-coupon discount instruments.
  • Tenors: 91, 182 and 364 days only. Distractors seen in PYQs: 271, 273, 274, 94.
  • Minimum ₹25,000 and multiples. Multiple-price auctions on e-Kuber. Non-competitive bids up to 5% of the notified amount.
  • Cash Management Bills (CMBs): under 91 days, to cover the Government's temporary cash mismatches.
  • T-bills are SLR-eligible.
T-bill yield = (Face value − Price) ÷ Price × 365 ÷ days × 100.
A 91-day bill at ₹98.50: 1.5 ÷ 98.5 × 365 ÷ 91 = 6.11%.

4. Certificate of Deposit (CD)

  • A negotiable, unsecured money-market deposit instrument, issued in demat form.
  • Issuers: SCBs (not RRBs) — including SFBs — and select All-India FIs. Co-operative banks and RRBs cannot issue CDs.
  • Minimum ₹5 lakh, in multiples of ₹5 lakh.
  • Tenor: banks 7 days to 1 year; FIs 1 to 3 years.
  • Issued at a discount, redeemed at par (face value).
  • Banks cannot lend against CDs. CRR and SLR apply to CDs (they are bank liabilities).
  • OTC trades must be reported within 15 minutes on F-TRAC (CCIL).

5. Commercial Paper (CP)

  • An unsecured promissory note issued at a discount.
  • Issuers: companies, NBFCs/HFCs, AIFIs.
  • Tenor 7 days to 1 year. Minimum ₹5 lakh and multiples.
  • Minimum credit rating A3. An issuer raising ₹1,000 crore or more in a year needs ratings from two CRAs.
  • IIBF book: tangible net worth at least ₹4 crore. A bank acts as the Issuing & Paying Agent (IPA).

6. Repo, market repo and tri-party repo

  • Repo: sell securities now with an agreement to repurchase later at a higher price — a collateralised loan. The seller is the borrower. Reverse repo is the same deal seen from the lender's side.
  • Market repo in G-secs, T-bills, SDLs and corporate bonds, among banks, PDs, MFs, insurers, NBFCs and others. A haircut is applied to the collateral.
  • Tri-party repo: a third-party agent handles collateral selection, payment & settlement, and custody & management.
    • Agent eligibility: at least ₹25 crore paid-up capital.
    • CCIL's TREPS (Tri-party Repo Dealing & Settlement, Nov 2018) replaced CBLO.

7. Bill Rediscounting Scheme (BRDS) and LTRO

  • BRDS: a bank that has discounted genuine trade bills rediscounts them with another bank or FI to raise short-term funds. The bill is discounted twice ("double discounting"). Only genuine trade bills are eligible, not accommodation bills.
  • LTRO (Feb 2020) and TLTRO (Mar 2020): RBI repos of 1-year and 3-year tenor at the repo rate, to improve transmission and credit. TLTRO funds went to corporate bonds, CP and NCDs (TLTRO 2.0: 50% to small/mid NBFCs and MFIs).
Traps:
  • The money market is up to 1 year; an SDL is NOT a money-market instrument.
  • Notice money runs up to 14 days, not 7.
  • CDs: co-op banks and RRBs cannot issue; SFBs can.
  • CP minimum rating is A3, not A2.
  • Both CDs and CPs are issued at a discount and redeemed at par.
  • NBFCs are not call-market participants.

1. Primary vs secondary market

The primary market is where securities are issued for the first time: the company gets the money. The secondary market is where existing securities trade between investors on stock exchanges (an auction/order-driven market) — it provides liquidity and price discovery. Both deal in equity and debt. The capital market also includes private placements.

  • Price discovered within a band (cap ≤ 120% of floor).

  • Retail individual investor: applies for up to ₹2 lakh.
  • Green shoe option: over-allotment of up to 15% of the issue, used by a stabilising agent to support the post-listing price (normally within 30 days).
  • ASBA (Application Supported by Blocked Amount): money is blocked in the investor's bank account (UPI mandate for retail) and debited only on allotment. Mandatory for public and rights issues. Listing in T+3 days.

4. Offer documents

  • DRHP: filed with SEBI for observations.
  • RHP: used in book building and filed with the RoC at least 3 days before the issue opens. It has full disclosures (business, financials, risk factors, objects, industry overview, promoters) but no final price or quantity.

5. Eligibility (main-board IPO, ICDR Reg 6(1) — profitability route)

In each of the preceding 3 years: net tangible assets ≥ ₹3 crore and net worth ≥ ₹1 crore; average operating profit ≥ ₹15 crore over those 3 years. Companies not meeting this use Reg 6(2) with at least 75% to QIBs.

6. Intermediaries in a public issue

Lead managers / BRLMs (merchant bankers) · registrar & share transfer agent · bankers to the issue (and sponsor bank for UPI) · syndicate members / brokers · underwriters · debenture trustee (for debt) · credit rating agencies · depositories · legal advisers. All are registered with SEBI.

1. Government securities

  • Tradeable debt of the Central or State Governments. They are "gilt-edged" — no credit risk.
  • Central Government: T-bills (short term, money market) and dated securities (long term).
  • State Governments: SDLs (State Development Loans), dated.

    • "When Issued" trading between announcement and issue; non-residents may take only long positions.

2. Primary Dealers (PDs, since 1995)

  • Authorised and regulated by RBI (not SEBI).
  • Obligations: underwrite primary auctions, bid in auctions, act as market makers with two-way quotes, and meet a minimum turnover ratio.
  • Standalone PD NOF: ₹150 crore. Bank-PDs run PD business departmentally.
  • PDs can borrow in the call market up to 225% of NOF.

3. Market infrastructure

  • NDS-OM (2005): RBI's anonymous screen-based order-matching system for secondary trading in G-secs, T-bills and SDLs (not corporate bonds). CCIL is the central counterparty. Banks, PDs, insurers, MFs and others access it; retail investors through RDS or brokers.
  • FIMMDA (Fixed Income Money Market & Derivatives Association, 1998): a voluntary self-regulatory body of banks, FIs, PDs and insurers for bond, money and derivatives markets. It sets market practices, documentation and valuation norms, and co-promoted FBIL.
  • FBIL (2014): publishes benchmarks — MIBOR, T-bill and G-sec curves, FX reference rates.

4. RBI Retail Direct Scheme (Nov 2021)

  • Individual retail investors, including NRIs eligible under FEMA, open a free Retail Direct Gilt (RDG) account with RBI. Companies are not eligible.
  • Primary auctions: non-competitive bids. Secondary trades: NDS-OM odd-lot/RFQ segments.
  • Instruments: GoI dated securities, T-bills, SDLs, SGBs. No corporate bonds.
  • Requirements: rupee SB account, PAN, KYC, e-mail and mobile number.

5. Bond valuation and theorems

Bond price = present value of all coupons + present value of the face value, discounted at the market yield (YTM).

  • If coupon = yield → price = par. If yield > coupon → discount. If yield < coupon → premium.
  • Current yield = annual coupon ÷ market price. YTM = the IRR of holding the bond to maturity.
Malkiel's bond theorems:
  1. Price moves inversely to yield.
  2. Longer maturity → larger price change for a given yield change.
  3. That sensitivity rises with maturity, but at a decreasing rate.
  4. The price rise for a yield fall is greater than the price fall for an equal yield rise (convexity).
  5. Lower coupon → higher price sensitivity.
Worked example: a ₹100 bond, 8% coupon, 1 year left, market yield 10% → price ≈ 108 ÷ 1.10 = ₹98.18 (discount). Current yield at that price = 8 ÷ 98.18 = 8.15%.

6. Corporate bonds and ICDs

  • Corporate bonds / debentures are regulated by SEBI.
    • Credit rating is mandatory for public issues; a debenture trustee is required (for maturity over 18 months, per the book).
    • Private placements go through the Electronic Book Provider (EBP) platform.
    • Repo in corporate bonds is allowed. Companies raise long-term funds this way.
  • Inter-Corporate Deposits (ICDs) are unsecured short-term loans or deposits between companies, governed by Companies Act Sec 186 limits. Banks cannot finance NBFCs for making ICDs.

  • PDs are registered with RBI.
  • Longer maturity means MORE sensitivity, and so does a lower coupon.
  • Retail Direct: no companies, no corporate bonds.
  • Name format is "7.25% GOI 2033", not "GOI 7.25%".
  • SDL coupon is half-yearly.
  • Settlement T+1 means the next WORKING day (a Friday deal settles Monday).

1. Profile and characteristics

The forex market is where currencies are exchanged. It is the world's largest and most liquid market, and works as a decentralised OTC network (not an exchange) running 24 hours, 5 days a week across time zones.

  • Currencies always trade in pairs (USD/INR).
  • Main costs are the bid–ask spread; there are traditionally no other service charges.
  • Features: liquidity, promptness, availability (24-hour), absolute freedom to open and close positions.

2. Evolution in India

  1. FERA 1947, made stricter in 1973 — exchange control.
  2. LERMS 1992 — dual exchange rate.
  3. Unified market-determined rate, March 1993.
  4. Current-account convertibility, Aug 1994 (IMF Article VIII).
  5. Tarapore Committees on capital-account convertibility (1997, 2006).
  6. FEMA 1999 (in force 1 June 2000) — exchange management instead of control.
  7. LRS: up to US$ 250,000 per year for resident individuals.

3. Participants and quotes

  • Participants:
    • RBI (regulator; intervenes to curb volatility).
    • Authorised Dealers: Cat I banks; Cat II (e.g., money changers with remittance rights); Cat III (select FIs). Also full-fledged money changers.
    • Corporates (exporters, importers), FPIs, brokers, investment banks, sovereign funds, individual customers.
  • Direct quote (₹ per unit of foreign currency, e.g., USD 1 = ₹85) is used in India.
  • Value dates: cash/ready T+0 · tom T+1 · spot T+2 · forward = beyond spot (up to and beyond 1 year).

5. FEDAI

  • Foreign Exchange Dealers' Association of India, 1958 — a self-regulatory association of Authorised Dealer banks (public, private, foreign, co-operative). Brokers are accredited, not members.
  • Functions: rules for handling forex business (interbank and merchant), training bank staff, accrediting forex brokers, announcing daily and periodic rates to members, advising RBI.
  • Co-promoter of FBIL.

6. FEMA, 1999

  • A civil law (FERA was criminal). It facilitates external trade and payments and orderly forex markets.
  • Current-account transactions are free, subject to reasonable restrictions. Capital-account transactions are regulated by RBI and the Government.
  • Enforcement: Directorate of Enforcement (Department of Revenue, Ministry of Finance).

1. Meaning

A derivative is a contract whose value is derived from an underlying: a share or index, interest rate, exchange rate, commodity (including agricultural commodities and metals), bond or credit event. RBI's definition has three parts:

  1. Its value changes with the underlying.
  2. It needs little or no initial net investment.
  3. It is settled at a future date.

The underlying should have a clear market price.

Bank example: an exporter expects USD 1 million in 3 months. The bank books a forward contract to sell USD at a fixed rate, so a falling dollar won't hurt.

2. History and market

  • Forward and futures trading: Chicago Board of Trade (1848).
  • India:
    • Index futures (June 2000, BSE and NSE), then index and stock options and stock futures (2001).
    • Currency futures (2008).
    • Interest-rate futures (relaunched 2009/2014).
    • OTC forex and interest-rate derivatives with banks.
  • India's exchange-traded equity options market is among the world's largest by number of contracts.

  • Participants: hedgers (cut risk), speculators (take risk for profit), arbitrageurs (exploit price differences), plus market makers.
  • Functions: risk transfer and hedging, price discovery, liquidity, lower transaction costs, access to otherwise unavailable markets.
  • Drawbacks: excessive speculation, leverage, counterparty and systemic risk.

OptionBuyer pays a premium for the right but not the obligation. Call = right to buy; put = right to sell, at the strike price. The writer (seller) has the obligation. American = exercisable any time up to expiry; European = only on expiry. ITM / ATM / OTM. Open interest = contracts outstanding
SwapExchange of cash flows: interest-rate swap (fixed ↔ floating, e.g., MIBOR OIS); currency swap (principal and interest in two currencies)
FRALocks in an interest rate for a future period. "a × b" = starts in a months, ends in b months. To borrow for 6 months starting 3 months from now → a 3 × 9 FRA

6. Credit Default Swaps (CDS)

  • The protection buyer pays a periodic premium (spread) to the protection seller. If a credit event hits the reference entity (default, bankruptcy, restructuring), the seller compensates the buyer. It transfers credit risk without selling the bond.
  • RBI (Credit Derivatives) Directions 2022:
    • Market makers (can buy and sell protection): SCBs — but not payment banks, SFBs, LABs or RRBs; NBFCs and HFCs meeting net-worth criteria; standalone PDs; AIFIs (EXIM, NABARD, NHB, SIDBI).
    • Users may buy protection, largely to hedge.
    • Reference obligations: CPs, CDs, NCDs, rated bonds etc. Trades are reported to the trade repository.

7. Documentation — ISDA

OTC derivatives use the ISDA Master Agreement (International Swaps and Derivatives Association). It comprises the Master Agreement, a Schedule, a Confirmation for each deal, and a Credit Support Annex for collateral. It standardises default events, netting and close-out.

Traps:
  • Derivatives need low or NO initial investment.
  • Forwards have flexible maturities; futures are standardised and need margins.
  • Put = right to SELL; the writer has the obligation.
  • American = anytime.
  • FRA "3 × 9", not "6 × 3".
  • Payment banks cannot be CDS market makers.

1. Factoring

A business sells or assigns its receivables (book debts) to a factor for an immediate advance (typically 80–90% of the invoice). The factor also manages the sales ledger, collects from buyers and may cover credit risk.

  • India: the Kalyanasundaram Committee (1988) recommended factoring. SBI Factors and Canbank Factors were set up in 1991.
  • The Factoring Regulation Act 2011 was amended in 2021 to let more NBFCs factor and to require receivables to be registered with CERSAI.

International factoring:

  • Two-factor system: the export factor finances and the import factor (in the buyer's country) assesses and collects.

  • Direct export factoring: the export factor deals directly with the importer, with no import factor.
  • Direct import factoring: the exporter deals directly with the import factor.

Fees: discount charge (interest on the advance), service/administration fee (% of invoice), and a credit-protection fee for non-recourse. Advantages: liquidity, credit protection, collection work outsourced, better cash cycle.

2. Forfaiting

Financing of medium/long-term export receivables (e.g., capital goods on deferred payment): the forfaiter buys the exporter's bills or promissory notes, usually avalised or guaranteed by the importer's bank, at a discount, without recourse, for 100% of the value at a fixed rate.

  1. Exporter and importer agree deferred terms.
  2. Importer's bank avalises the notes.
  3. Exporter sells the notes to the forfaiter and gets cash.
  4. Forfaiter collects at maturity.

Fees: discount, commitment fee and option fee. Advantages: converts a credit sale into a cash sale, removes credit, transfer and interest-rate risk, frees credit lines.

3. TReDS (Trade Receivables Discounting System)

  • RBI-authorised electronic platforms under the PSS Act 2007, to finance MSME receivables from large buyers. Examples: RXIL, Invoicemart (A.TReDS), M1xchange.
  • Eligibility to set up a TReDS: minimum paid-up capital ₹25 crore; promoters can't be buyers, sellers or financiers on the platform.
  • Participants:

    • Buyers: corporates, PSUs, Government departments.
    • Financiers: banks, NBFC-Factors and other RBI-permitted FIs.
    • 2023 Insurance companies as the 4th participant (credit insurance).
  • Process:
    1. The MSME uploads an invoice — a "factoring unit" (FU).
    2. The buyer accepts it.
    3. Financiers bid; the MSME picks the best bid.
    4. Funds reach the MSME (T+1).
    5. The buyer pays the financier on the due date.
    All without recourse to the MSME. Secondary-market trading of FUs is allowed (2023). A seller upload is factoring; a buyer upload is reverse factoring.

  • Venture capital: long-term, mostly equity finance to new, innovative, high-risk, high-growth businesses (often technology start-ups) that cannot get bank loans. The VC also brings management participation and mentoring. It is high-risk, high-return; there is no collateral and no guaranteed return.
