Syllabus: Lease finance · Evolution · Types · Pros & cons · Impact on ratios · Legal & regulatory aspects · Hire purchase · Parties · Legal aspects · Leasing vs HP. 13 PYQs.

1. Leasing

The owner (lessor) gives the right to use an asset to a user (lessee) for periodic rentals; ownership stays with the lessor. In India, First Leasing Company of India (Chennai, 1973) was the first leasing company.

Finance (capital) leaseOperating lease
Long term, non-cancellable; full payout of cost plus return; risks and rewards pass to the lessee; the lessee maintains the assetShort term, cancellable; the lessor recovers cost from several lessees; the lessor maintains it and bears obsolescence. Used for computers, aircraft, windmills, servers

Other types:

  • Sale and lease-back: sell your asset and lease it back.
  • Leveraged lease: the lessor borrows part of the price from a lender.
  • Direct lease; cross-border lease (e.g., an aircraft leased to a UAE airline).
  • Wet lease (with crew) vs dry lease.
  • Advantages: 100% financing, conserves capital, tax-deductible rentals, flexibility, protection from obsolescence (operating). Disadvantages: no ownership or residual value, often costlier, the lessor can repossess.
  • Impact on ratios (book view, old accounting): rentals are off the balance sheet, so the debt-equity ratio is unchanged and the lessee looks better than a borrower. Under Ind AS 116, most leases now come on the balance sheet (right-of-use asset + lease liability).
  • Legal: a lease of movables is a contract of bailment under the Indian Contract Act. Regulatory: NBFCs doing leasing are regulated by RBI (now NBFC-ICC); banks may lease departmentally or through subsidiaries.

2. Hire purchase

Goods are hired with an option to buy. The hirer gets possession at once and pays instalments (principal + interest). Ownership passes on payment of the last instalment. On default, the owner can repossess.

  • Parties: hire vendor / owner, hirer, and often a financier. Hire Purchase Act 1972 (never brought into force); governed by contract and bailment law.
  • Tax: the hirer claims depreciation and the interest component as an expense.
  • Suitable for movable tangible goods (vehicles, machinery, consumer durables), not intangibles like goodwill.
  • HP is not an instalment sale: in an instalment sale, ownership passes at once.

Syllabus: Credit rating, CRAs, history, characteristics, importance, benefits, factors, process, symbols, outlook, regulation, fees · Credit scoring · CICs, membership, guidelines, scores · Ratings vs scores. 11 PYQs.

1. Credit rating

  • A credit rating is an opinion on the relative ability and willingness of an issuer to meet a specific debt obligation on time. It is not a buy/sell recommendation or a guarantee. It is instrument-specific and dynamic.
  • History: Moody's (1909, USA). In India: CRISIL 1987 (first), ICRA 1991 (promoted by IFCI), CARE 1993, India Ratings (Fitch), Brickwork, Acuité, Infomerics.
  • Regulated by SEBI (CRA Regulations 1999). RBI recognises some for bank capital (ECAIs). Fees are paid by the issuer.
  • Benefits: investors judge risk cheaply; issuers get wider access and better pricing; regulators use ratings; banks use them for risk weights.
  • Factors considered: business risk (industry, market position), financial risk (leverage, cash flows, coverage), management quality, governance, project risk.
  • Process:
    1. Issuer's request and mandate.
    2. Analyst team collects information.
    3. Management meetings and site visits.
    4. Rating committee decides.
    5. Rating communicated to the issuer (who may appeal).
    6. Published.
    7. Surveillance till maturity.
  • Outlook: positive, negative, stable or developing (likely direction over 1–2 years). Credit watch = an event may change the rating soon.

1. Structure and regulation

  • A mutual fund pools many investors' money and invests it as per a stated objective. It is set up as a trust.
  • Structure: Sponsor → Trustees (protect unit-holders) → AMC, appointed by the trustees, which manages the portfolio (asset allocation, buying and selling, liquidity) and needs a minimum net worth set by SEBI. A custodian holds the securities; the AMC does not own them. An RTA keeps investor records.
  • Regulator: SEBI (MF Regulations 1996). AMFI (1995) is the industry association.

2. Evolution

  • Phase I: UTI 1963 — set up by the Government to develop MFs; first scheme US-64.
  • Phase II: public-sector MFs from 1987 (SBI MF first).
  • Phase III: private MFs from 1993 (Kothari Pioneer first).
  • Phase IV: UTI bifurcated (2003), growth via SIPs and "Mutual Funds Sahi Hai".

3. Classification

  • By structure: open-ended (buy or redeem any time), close-ended (fixed maturity, listed), interval.
  • By asset (SEBI 2017 categorisation): equity (large cap = top 100 companies, mid = 101–250, small = 251 onwards; multi-cap ≥ 65% equity across caps; ELSS 3-year lock-in), debt (liquid ≤ 91 days, gilt ≥ 80% G-secs, floater ≥ 65% floating-rate), hybrid, solution-oriented, others (index fund / ETF ≥ 95% in the index; fund of funds ≥ 95% in other funds).

4. Key terms

  • NFO: a new scheme's first offer.
  • NAV = (market value of assets − liabilities) ÷ units outstanding. Declared daily for open-ended schemes. Book: 4 decimals for debt/index, 2 for equity.
  • Expense ratio (TER): annual cost as % of AUM, capped by SEBI. Direct plans (2013) have a lower TER.
  • Load: entry load is banned (since Aug 2009); an exit load may apply.
  • Riskometer: 6 levels — Low, Low to Moderate, Moderate, Moderately High, High, Very High.
  • Risks: market, interest-rate, credit, liquidity, concentration.
  • Strategies: SIP (rupee-cost averaging), SWP (systematic withdrawal), STP (switch).
  • Role in the capital market: mobilise retail savings, add institutional depth, provide liquidity, professional management.

Syllabus: Overview of financial markets (meaning, evolution, segments, functions, price discovery) · Interconnection of markets — process, reasons, importance, heterogeneity, market integration in India, levels, Asian Clearing Union, benefits & costs, interconnectedness of money/credit/capital/forex markets, integrated treasury, contagion.

1. Financial markets

  • A financial market is any mechanism — not necessarily a physical place — through which buyers and sellers trade money, securities, commodities and currencies, and prices are formed. It needs buyers, sellers, instruments and pricing, but no fixed location.
  • Segments: money (≤ 1 year) · capital (equity and debt, primary and secondary) · forex · derivatives · commodity · credit/insurance markets.
  • Functions: mobilising savings into productive uses; price discovery; liquidity; lower transaction and information costs; risk sharing. They do not guarantee returns.
  • Price discovery depends on supply and demand, risk attitudes, volatility, available information and market mechanisms.

2. Interconnectedness

Markets are linked: rates and prices in one move quickly into others. Global markets are linked too, so shocks in one country ripple worldwide.

  • Reasons: deregulation and liberalisation, technology, capital flows, arbitrage, common participants (banks are active in all markets), financial innovation.
  • Levels: integration within domestic segments (money ↔ G-sec ↔ forex ↔ credit) and integration with global markets.
  • Benefits: efficient allocation of capital, better price discovery, deeper liquidity, diversification, lower cost of funds, smoother monetary transmission.
  • Costs / disadvantages: volatility, contagion (spread of crises — Asian crisis 1997, GFC 2008, taper tantrum 2013), less policy autonomy (the "impossible trinity").
  • Heterogeneity: markets differ in depth, participants and regulation, so integration is partial.
  • Typical linkages:
    • The call rate moves with the repo/LAF corridor.
    • Bond yields move with policy rates.
    • Equity prices usually move inversely to bond yields.
    • Forward premia track interest-rate differentials.
  • Integrated treasury: a bank manages its domestic (money, G-sec) and forex desks together — for liquidity, arbitrage, ALM and better pricing.

3. Asian Clearing Union (ACU)

Set up in 1974 (HQ Tehran) to settle payments among member central banks on a multilateral net basis, saving foreign exchange. Uses Asian Monetary Units. Members: Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, Iran, Maldives, Myanmar, Nepal, Pakistan, Sri Lanka. Afghanistan is not a member.

1. REITs (SEBI REIT Regulations 2014)

  • A trust that owns income-generating real estate (mostly offices and malls) and passes rental income to unit-holders. Units are listed and tradeable. First in the world: USA, 1960. First in India: Embassy Office Parks (2019).
  • Organisation: Sponsor (sets it up, minimum holding) · Manager (runs assets and investments) · Trustee (a SEBI-registered debenture trustee that holds assets for unit-holders) · Valuer.
  • Rules: at least 80% of value in completed, revenue-generating properties; distribute at least 90% of net distributable cash flows, at least half-yearly.
  • Types: equity REITs (own property), mortgage REITs (lend / hold MBS), hybrid REITs (both). By property: office, retail, residential, healthcare, hospitality, industrial/warehousing. (The book's "odd one out" list excludes industrial.)
  • REIT vs real-estate MF: a REIT owns property directly and earns rent; a real-estate MF invests in REIT units and real-estate company shares.
  • Advantages: regular income, small ticket size, liquidity, professional management, diversification. Disadvantages: market price volatility, interest-rate sensitivity, limited growth (most income is paid out).
  • Taxation: largely pass-through. Interest received is taxable for the unit-holder; dividend is exempt if the SPV hasn't opted for the concessional tax regime; capital gains apply on units as listed securities.

2. InvITs (SEBI InvIT Regulations 2014)

  • Pool money to own completed infrastructure assets that earn steady cash: roads (tolls/annuity), power transmission, telecom towers, fibre, gas pipelines. First: IRB InvIT (2017).
  • Rationale: developers recycle capital (asset monetisation) and investors get long-term yield. Part of the National Monetisation Pipeline.
  • Organisation: Sponsor · Investment Manager · Project Manager (runs the projects) · Trustee.
  • At least 80% in completed revenue-generating projects; distribute ≥ 90%.
  • Types: publicly offered (listed) and privately placed (listed or unlisted).
  • Revenue model: toll and annuity, transmission charges, tower rentals.
  • Regulator: SEBI. Taxation is similar to REITs (pass-through).
